text:
Education in New Zealand is a publicly funded, secular system providing free primary and secondary schooling from age five to nineteen for citizens and permanent residents. The system is primarily comprised of state schools, which are government-owned and operated, and state-integrated schools, which are government-funded but may charge compulsory attendance dues to cover maintenance costs while retaining a specific religious or philosophical character. Private schools operate independently, relying mainly on tuition fees and receiving limited government subsidies. Funding for state schools is allocated per-student based on decile ratings (socio-economic status) and school size, with additional resources provided for special needs students through the Ongoing Resource Scheme (ORS). Teachers are employed by the Ministry of Education and receive fixed, nationwide salaries, while students are expected to cover voluntary expenses such as uniforms, trips, and stationery.
The curriculum is standardized nationally under the New Zealand Curriculum (for English-medium schools) and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa (for Māori-medium schools), covering eight learning areas including English, mathematics, science, and the arts. While secondary education is generally compulsory until age 19, most students complete five years of high school (Years 9–13). Tertiary education is regulated by the New Zealand Qualifications Framework and includes universities, polytechnics, and vocational training institutions. Historically, the system has faced challenges regarding Māori language preservation and academic achievement, leading to significant reforms such as the establishment of kōhanga reo (language nests) and the recognition of Māori as an official language. Recent initiatives also aim to improve educational standards and address issues such as school bullying and the implementation of a new high school credit system.
